name: Yarrow
habitat: Disturbed sunny ground — roadsides, meadows, pasture, old fields, gravel. One of the most widespread temperate plants there is.
identify: Leaves finely divided into many tiny segments — feathery, almost fern-like; the species name means 'thousand-leaved'.
Leaves are strongly aromatic when crushed — a sharp, medicinal, slightly sweet smell.
Flat-topped cluster of small white (occasionally pink) flower heads on a single stiff stem, 30-60 cm.
Stem is round and hairy, NOT hollow, and has no purple blotching.

lookalikes.name: Poison hemlock
lookalikes.danger: Lethal. Ingestion causes ascending paralysis and respiratory failure; there is no field treatment.
lookalikes.tell: Hemlock has a HOLLOW stem with distinct PURPLE BLOTCHES, is hairless, grows much taller (up to 2-3 m), has broader lacy leaves, and smells foul and mousy rather than sweet and medicinal. Yarrow's stem is solid, hairy, unblotched.

lookalikes.name: Water hemlock
lookalikes.danger: Among the most poisonous plants in North America; a mouthful of root can be fatal.
lookalikes.tell: Grows in wet ground, has a stout chambered rootstock and broad toothed leaflets — nothing like yarrow's feathery foliage.

lookalikes.name: Queen Anne's lace / wild carrot
lookalikes.danger: Not deadly, but confusing it means you are in the carrot family and one step from hemlock.
lookalikes.tell: Carrot-scented, has a single dark floret at the centre of the umbel and bracts below it; yarrow's flower cluster has no bracts and smells medicinal.

preparations.method: Chew or crush fresh leaf and press it directly onto the wound; hold with a dressing.
preparations.for_use: Slowing bleeding from a minor cut or graze; the traditional battlefield use behind the old name 'soldier's woundwort'.

preparations.method: Dry leaf and flower, crumble to powder, keep dry.
preparations.for_use: Packing a shallow bleeding wound when nothing else is available.

preparations.method: Steep a handful of dried leaf in hot water for 10 minutes.
preparations.for_use: A wound wash, or drunk for fever.

cautions: The look-alike risk is the main danger here, and it is a fatal one — see the tells above before you touch it.
Asteraceae family: people allergic to ragweed, chrysanthemum or daisy can react to yarrow.
Avoid in pregnancy; it has traditional emmenagogue use.
Prolonged skin contact plus sun causes photosensitivity in some people.
It is a styptic for MINOR bleeding. It does not substitute for direct pressure on a serious wound.
evidence: Long and consistent traditional use as a styptic across Europe and North America; laboratory work supports antibacterial and anti-inflammatory activity. Clinical evidence for wound use is thin.
